lesson_output:
Standards

K.F.PA.6.a Isolate and pronounce initial, final, and then medial sounds in spoken words with three phonemes

K.F.P.1.a Identify and produce basic one-to-one phoneme-grapheme correspondences for the most frequently used sound for each consonant.

K.F.H.1.a Form all uppercase and lowercase letters.

K.F.P.3.a Use knowledge of letter/sound correspondences to connect letters (graphemes) to sounds (phonemes) to encode simple one-syllable words, including high-frequency words (VC, CV, CVC).

Objectives

Isolate and identify the initial and final /b/ sound in CVC words

Connect the letter b to its phoneme /b/

Write the letter b with accuracy

Apply knowledge of the /b/ sound and its grapheme to encode CVC words

**1. Review & Connect**

**\[Explanation**: "The purpose of this part of the lesson is to start with a quick review of previously learned sounds. Do not use sounds that have not been directly taught. Do not use words that have sounds that have not been directly taught."**\]**

**#Teacher Script:**

"Let's review our sounds. We are doing our *Sound Sparks* game. Look up here. When I point to a sound. You will all say that sound when I say go, and when you see my hand close to a fist."

"Ready. My Turn. {Teacher points to /m/.}

Get Ready. Go." (children chorally respond /m/).

Ready. My Turn. {Teacher points to /a/}

Get Ready. Go." (children chorally respond /a/).

{Teacher continues this process, reviewing previous sounds; sounds to preview to support later activities of the lesson = p, d, t, c, l, g, n, m, j; short a, e, i, o}

Here's you challenge. Now we are doing *Write that Sound.* I say the sound. You write the sound and show me when I say show me, and you see my hand close to fist.

My sound is /a/. Write the sound. Show me. (children hold up their whiteboards together)

My sound is /d/. Write the sound. Show me. (children hold up their whiteboards together)

+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Corrective Feedback: Some children may confuse the direction of d, writing instead b or p.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| Teacher: You are close. My sound is /d/. Everyone look up here. Some of you wrote this. {Teacher writes b}. This was our new sound we learned yesterday. This sound is /b/. We are writing /d/. This is /d/ {Teacher writes d on the board}. What is different about these two letters? Everyone think. Partner 1 tell Partner 2. Stop. Partner 2 tell Partner 1. Stop. Jesslyn, what is different about the /b/ and /d/? (child should respond that bottom bubble is different). |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| Exactly, both the /d/ and /b/ have a straight line down, but one has a bubble on the back, the left, and one has a bubble in the front, on the right. Everyone say /d/. Where's the bubble, on the front or back? Everyone (on the back). Everyone say /b/. Where's the bubble? Everyone. (on the front). \*Make sure to bring back d later in the review.                                                                                                                        |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

**2. Model, Explain, Engage**

**\[Explanation:** The purpose of this part of the lesson is to connect a sound or sound patterns that you focused on during your reading block to writing its corresponding grapheme patterns. First, make sure children clearly can distinguish the targeted sound; then, hook that sound to the letter patterns through modeling and explaining the sequence of strokes for letters and correct order of letters.**\]**

**#Teacher Script:**

We've been working on the /b/ sound.

Say the sound. (Children repeat sound)

Let's do our sound motion. Get Ready Go. (Children make a **two-hand grab**, then **throw forward**, saying /b/.)

We can hear /b/ at the beginning of words like ball, but we can also hear /b/ at the end of words like cab.

Let's do **Stretch the Sounds**, so we can practice how to listen for /b/ at the beginning or end.

My word is *big*. Stretch the Sounds. (children say each sound /b/ /i/ /g/, while holding up a finger for every sound, then repeat the word-*big*).

My word is cab. Strech the Sounds, (children say each sound /c/ /a/ /b/, while holding up a finger for every sound, then repeat the word-cab.

{Teacher provides 4-5 words}

+------------------------------------------------------------------+
| CVC words to use in this activity:                               |
|                                                                  |
| big, bin, bob, bog, bat, bed, bib, cab, job, lab, web, rib, cob  |
+------------------------------------------------------------------+

Now we are going to play our **Sound Hunt Game.** You are going to stretch those sounds to hunt for the /b/ sound. You are thinking, "Do you hear it at the beginning, or do you hear it at the end?" Each of you has a ball card because ball starts with the /b/ sound. You also have two boxes, one beginning box and one ending box{teacher points to elkonin box on left for beginning and right for the ending}.

We are listening for where the /b/ sound is at, the beginning or ending of the word. I will say a word, and if you hear the /b/ sound at the beginning, I want you to slide the ball into the beginning box {teacher demonstrates}

If you hear the /b/ sound at the end of the word, I want you to slide the ball into the ending spot {teacher demonstrates}. (*If you need extra modeling click here*)

+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Extra Modeling:                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
|                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| My turn: My word is cab. I am thinking to myself where do I hear the /b/ sound, at the beginning or the end of the word. First, I am going to stretch the sounds in my head: c-a-b. I hear /c/ at the beginning, but I hear /b/ at the end: c-a-b. So, I am going to slide my ball card into the ending box {teacher demonstrates}.  |
+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

Okay. Let's get started. My turn. The word is big. Get Ready. Show me. (children should have moved the ball card into the beginning box).

Perfect. The word big b---i---g starts with a /b/ sound. I don't hear /b/ at the end of the word big; I hear it at the beginning. Great job.

Alright put your listening ears on. My turn. The word is *web*. Get Ready. Show me. (children should have moved their ball card into the ending box). {Teacher repeats this process to cement sound to memory then connects to letter form}

Now let's think about writing the /b/ sound. The letter that matches the /b/ sound -- is the letter b.

Watch me closely. I will show you how to form lowercase b. No one is using their pencil yet or writing. You are watching me.

{teacher demonstrates on a visual that shows children the correct sequence of letter strokes and uses *sequence verbal cues*}.

***##Sequence Verbal Cues*** **for letter b: Straight line down; put a bubble on it.**

First, start at the top line. Straight line down. Lift up. Now put a bubble on it. {Teacher repeats as needed}

Say it with me as you watch.

Straight line down. Say It. (children repeat).

Put a bubble on it. Say it. (children repeat).

Now you say it as I write.

Ready. Go (Children repeat *straight line down, put on the belly* as teacher demonstrates the strokes). {Teacher repeats a few times}.

**3. Guided Practice**

**\[Explanation:** The purpose is to give children practice writing the letter while supporting proper pencil grip and correct sequence of stroke formation using handwriting lines.\]

**#Teacher Script:**

Let's practice how to write lowercase b. We are not using our pencils yet. Let's do our Magic Finger Write. Place your finger at the top of the line. Let me see {teacher checks students finger placement} Remember it's important when we are writing to try to touch the lines. The lines are there to help us.

Straight line down. (children move finger from top to bottom line)

Put on a belly. (children lift finger and add a bottom curve to the bottom)

{Repeat as needed}.

Now, pick up the pencil. Show me how you hold your pencil. Remember we slant our paper. Your free hand holds the paper.

Let's do our **Say and Write.** Say the steps as you write. Everyone put your pencil at the top line on the left. You want to start here. {Teacher points to top left-hand line}

Let me see. {Teacher corrects students if needed}. Ready. Say and write. Go. (Children write the letter as they say the verbal cues "Straight line down. Put on the belly.") {Teacher monitors children's letter writing}.

Now you are ready for **Write and Sound**. You are going to write the letter b, but this time you say the sound /b/ as you write. Everyone put your pencil at the top line. Ready. Write and Sound. Go. (Children write the letter as they say the sound /b/) {Teacher monitors children's letter writing}.

**4. Application**

\[**Explanation:** The purpose of this part of the lesson is to facilitate children's spelling of the letter or letter patterns when they hear the sound(s). This supports children's early coordination of matching sound to letter(s) for the purpose of spelling words.\]

**#Teacher Script:**

Boys and girls, remember stretch the sounds. Now I am going to say a word. You are going to stretch those sounds and spell the word. We are doing three sound words. Consonant-vowel-consonant. I am going to remind you of the vowels you know so far {Teacher displays the a, e, i, and o vowels}

Where are we going to hear these vowels, the beginning, middle, or end of the word? Everyone. Right. These are the vowels you hear in the middle of the word. We are going to do stretch and spell. You are going to stretch the sounds of word. Look at your Stretch-Sound handwriting paper. {Teacher directs students' attention to the handwriting sheet}. How many sounds will we hear if these are CVC words. Everyone. Yes. three sounds. That's why we see three boxes for each sound. You first stretch the sounds, then write the letter for each sound. Let me show you. My turn. The word is cab. So, I first stretch the sounds, c-a-b, the beginning sound is /c/. I know that the /c/ sound is written with the letter c. I am going to write c in the first block. So, we have /c/-/a/. The /a/ sound is written with the letter a, so I write the letter a, remember that's our vowel, in the middle box. So, we have /c/-/a/-/b/. That's our new sound at the end. I am going to write the letter b for the /b/ sound in the last box. Okay. Let\'s try.

My turn. My first word is bin. Stretch the sound everyone.

First sound. Write the letter

Second sound. Write the letter.

Third sound. Write the letter.

{Teacher uses the same list of words that were used in the Sound Hunt activity above. Teacher monitors students' answers providing corrective feedback.}

**5. Wrap-Up**

**\[Explanation:** The purpose of this part of the lesson is to remind students what they were focused on and provide praise for their accomplishments**\].**

**#Teacher Script:**

Alright, boys and girls I am so proud of you. What sound have we been working on in our spelling? (Children respond /b/).

Perfect! And what letter do we write for the /b/ sound. (Children respond "b").

Show and tell me how to write b (children air write with *sequence verbal cues*--e.g., straight line down, put on the belly)

Wonderful! Kiss your brains.
source_note: Further Lesson 1: /b/ beginning+ending, full CVC spelling
